title: Interconnect noise floor and tail latency correlation study
content:
Summary:

This is an internal investigation into how low-amplitude, persistent interconnect activity (what we call the "interconnect noise floor") correlates with tail-latency excursions during multi-GPU LLM inference. The study focuses on mixed tensor/pipeline-parallel LLM serving, NCCL traffic patterns, and the sensitivity of tail P95/P99 latency to small background transfers and host-side DMA bursts.

Motivation / why we did this:
- Operators report intermittent tail-latency spikes on nodes that otherwise look healthy (no CPU saturation, normal GPU util).
- Existing microburst analyses explain large spikes, but not the small-yet-frequent tails observed in certain racks/regions.
- Hypothesis: sustained low-level background traffic (e.g., periodic KV-cache prefetches, logging/telemetry, backup jobs, or noisy co-tenants) increases serialization delays in the interconnect and NCCL, raising tail percentiles for time-sensitive requests.

Hypotheses tested:
H1: A persistent low-bandwidth background transfer (~50-200 MB/s per link) increases P95/P99 latency for small interactive requests by creating queueing at switch/host buffers.
H2: Background traffic that is bursty but below microburst thresholds still increases serialization variance due to NCCL progress scheduling and PCIe read amplification.
H3: Placement of pipeline stages across NVLink/NVSwitch vs across PCIe+RoCE links changes the sensitivity to the noise floor; cross-host placements are most sensitive.

Testbed and environment:
- 4 homogeneous nodes per experiment; each node: 8x A100-40GB, PCIe 4.0 host, dual 100GbE RoCE links, NVSwitch fully connected per node.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.1, NCCL 2.18 (tuned builds), kernel 6.1 with cq-poll tuning applied in some runs.
- Serving runtime: local branch noise-floor-experiments (commit: 9b8c3f), with tracing hooks for NCCL ops and host bytes-in-flight telemetry.
- Workloads: small-chat (prompt len 32, gen len 64), long-chat (prompt 512, gen 512), and kv-prefetch synthetic pattern (periodic 8MB fetch every 300ms).
- Measuring: per-request latency histogram (client-side), per-GPU NVLink counters, per-host PCIe read/write bytes/sec, switch port utilization summaries, NCCL op latency (all traced), and kernel scheduling stalls.

Methodology:
- Baseline runs: no synthetic background traffic, run 30k small-chat requests with concurrency sweep (1..64).
- Noise-floor injection: create steady traffic at 50MB/s, 100MB/s, 200MB/s per inter-node link using a micro-transfer tool that models KV-cache prefetch behavior (many small reads evenly spaced vs fewer medium transfers).
- Bursty-noise runs: keep average rate same but cluster transfers into short windows (e.g., 10ms bursts every 300ms).
- Placement matrix: colocated pipeline stages (all NVSwitch intra-node), split across PCIe within host, and cross-host pipeline splits (NVLink->RoCE).
- Repeat each experiment 5 times; capture outlier runs for manual trace analysis.

Key results (high-level):
- Even at 50MB/s per link sustained background load, small-chat P95 increased by ~12% and P99 by ~28% for cross-host pipeline splits.
- Colocated intra-node NVSwitch placements showed <5% increase in P95 and ~10% P99 at 200MB/s, indicating NVSwitch is more resilient to low-level noise than RoCE+PCIe paths for these workloads.
- Bursty noise with identical mean rate produced higher tail impact than evenly spaced transfers. Example: 100MB/s clustered bursts (10ms every 300ms) caused P99 to jump 2–3x compared to steady 100MB/s.
- NCCL op traces show that contention manifests as increased NCCL barrier wait times and longer small-allreduce requeue latencies; the serving runtime's async-progress loop sometimes observed ~1–3ms extra latency per collective under noise conditions.
- Host staging and PCIe read amplification correlated strongly with tail spikes for cross-host pipeline layouts: when host DMA queued due to small bursts, token-generation critical path waits for KV cache reads increased.

Representative numbers (small-chat, concurrency=8):
- Baseline: P50=16ms, P95=42ms, P99=68ms
- 50MB/s steady (cross-host): P50=17ms, P95=47ms (+12%), P99=87ms (+28%)
- 100MB/s bursty (cross-host): P50=18ms, P95=61ms (+45%), P99=180ms (+165%)
- 200MB/s steady (intra-node NVSwitch): P50=17ms, P95=43ms (+2%), P99=75ms (+10%)

Observations and interpretation:
- Small persistent traffic creates queueing at NIC and switch egress, but the dominant effect for tails is the interaction between that queueing and the serving runtime's synchronization points (NCCL collectives, KV cache reads).
- Bursty traffic is worse because it aligns with request bursts and can cause short-lived saturation of PCIe/NVLink drivers, triggering retransmits/retries or NIC queuing that cascades into NCCL slowdown.
- Intra-node NVSwitch keeps most hot data on the fast fabric, reducing PCIe round-trips and host DMA dependence; therefore placement of pipeline stages matters a lot for tail sensitivity.
- Kernel scheduling and cq-poll frequency on the host impacted how quickly small transfers were drained; more aggressive polling reduced tails but increased host CPU cost.

Actionable mitigations tested (and results):
1) NCCL tuning: lowering NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME aggressiveness and enabling NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING reduced requeue latency variability by ~10% in pathological runs.
2) Traffic shaping: applying an egress policer at 100MB/s per link for non-critical flows (telemetry, backups) eliminated most persistent-noise effects while keeping peak utilization available for inference bursts.
3) Placement rules: prefer NVSwitch-local pipeline placement when possible for latency-sensitive routes; fallback to cross-host only when capacity requires it.
4) Host polling tuning: increasing cq-poll frequency to 1ms reduced P99 by ~15% under steady noise but increased baseline host CPU usage by ~2.5%.
5) Micro-scheduling change: transiently relax collective barrier strictness for KV-cache prefetches (make them opportunistic) — resulted in lower P99 but requires careful correctness auditing.

Recommendations for product and infra:
- Short term: add a noise-floor detector to alert when sustained low-level inter-node traffic exceeds a threshold (e.g., 50MB/s sustained per link). This should appear in the Console as an optional latency risk signal.
- Mid term: scheduler rule to bias sensitive routes toward NVSwitch-local placements and to avoid known noisy racks. Integrate with placement hints in the model manifest.
- Long term: build adaptive traffic shaping in the fabric (or via top-of-rack policing) to reserve headroom for inference tails; and add runtime-level graceful-degradation policies that can temporarily throttle non-critical prefetch/telemetry during latency-sensitive windows.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Quantify how common production noisy neighbors are (need cluster-wide telemetry sampling) — instrument 10% of production pods for 2 weeks.
- Validate micro-scheduling change correctness across model variants (transformer/decoder-only vs mixture-of-experts).
- Explore if smarter prefetch pacing (align to generation steps) can provide tail safety without losing cache hit-rate.
- Measure effect on throughput/overall cost of more aggressive host polling at fleet scale.

Known limitations of this study:
- Testbed is homogeneous and synthetic; production racks show more heterogeneity (different switch firmware, microcode).
- Background noise was generated via our micro-transfer tool; real co-tenant behavior may differ in packetization and priority handling.
- We did not exhaustively sweep all NCCL versions and vendor driver variants (only 2.18 on this testbed).

Next experiments planned:
- Fleet sampling for real-world noise floors and correlating with request traces (INF-3421).
- Test with RoCE priority flow control (PFC) toggled to see if strict pause frames mitigate or worsen tails.
- Longer-duration production smoke run where non-critical flows are egress-shaped to measure impact on model QoS and background job completion time.

Appendix (notes & traces):
- Trace examples and heatmaps are attached in the Jira ticket INF-3421.
- Quick reproduction: branch noise-floor-experiments, run scripts/bench/run_noise_sweep.sh --workload small-chat --concurrency 8 --inject-rate 100MBps --burst-pattern clustered.
- Author notes: During analysis we observed that certain switch firmwares with older buffer-management heuristics amplified the effect; coordinate with infra to get firmware inventory.

If you want to dig into particular trace logs or reproduce on a smaller dev rig, ping me or schedule a session — I can walk through the perf traces and the NCCL timelines.
